title: The Bosphorus Brief — 14 October 2026
overview: The day's most consequential news for residents is judicial, not geopolitical: an Istanbul court again declined to act on the European Court of Human Rights' Kavala ruling, a pattern European judges elsewhere criticized directly. Regional tension around Yemen and Saudi Arabia continues, but so far has not translated into new travel restrictions in Türkiye. On the money side, the lira held steady and fund-crisis investors got a repayment timeline.

sections.heading: Kavala case: ECHR ruling still not applied
sections.body: An Istanbul court rejected Osman Kavala's request for release and retrial, despite a European Court of Human Rights ruling calling for exactly that. Independent outlets Bianet and Medyascope both describe the decision plainly as non-compliance with the ECHR; international outlets Euronews and DW covered it the same way, with no divergence in framing across lenses this time. Separately, European judges criticized Turkish courts for what they called rubber-stamping of prison visit recordings in related proceedings. For foreign residents, the case remains the clearest live marker of how domestic courts weigh Strasbourg rulings — worth watching if you have any pending ECHR-linked matter.

sections.heading: Fund crisis repayments get a timeline
sections.body: President Erdoğan said repayments of up to 1 million lira (about $20,000) to investors caught in Turkey's fund crisis will begin this month, once parliament passes the governing legislation. If you or someone you know had money tied up in affected funds, watch for the legislation's passage before expecting disbursement — no exact date has been set yet.

sections.heading: Greece extradition pressure, Azerbaijan headscarf dispute
sections.body: Turkey is pressing Greece to extradite individuals linked to the Gülen movement, a recurring diplomatic request covered by opposition-leaning outlets. Separately, Azerbaijan's ruling party publicly accused the AKP of stoking division over Baku's school headscarf ban — a rare public rebuke between the two governments, reported mainly by opposition-leaning and independent outlets. Neither story changes anything procedurally for residents today, but both are useful context for the region's shifting diplomatic tone.

sections.heading: Yemen-Saudi exchange continues; no new travel guidance
sections.body: The Saudi-led coalition struck a fuel depot near Sanaa; Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh were intercepted, with Saudi authorities reporting minor injuries from debris. Oil prices rose on the news. Separately, Trump suggested Turkey is already providing some support in the Yemen conflict. None of this has altered US travel advisory levels — Türkiye remains Level 2, and the Gulf-adjacent countries show no new changes — but it's part of why oil and lira-watchers are paying closer attention this week.

closing: Stay dry out there, and as always, keep your ikamet paperwork a photo away on your phone — just in case.
